4. The law on the point is well settled. Section 5 of the limitation Act enables a Court to admit an appeal after the period of Limitation prescribed therefor when the appellant satisfies the Court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring it within the prescribed period. In the case of Province of East Pakistan Vs. Abdul Hamid Darji and others, 1970 SCMR 558(562), Hamudur Rahman, C. J. speaking for the Court observed; 

 As to the legal aspect of the question, namely, as to what is or is not sufficient cause for the purpose of an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, it is manifest that no hard and fast rule can be laid down, nor is it desirable that this should be done. Each case has to the considered on its own facts. What may be sufficient in one case may not be sufficient in another case, but this much is certain that here, by lapse of time, a valuable right has accrued to the other side, it should not be lightly taken away. 

 This Court has further more repeatedly pointed out that in an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, it is the duty of the party seeking condonation to explain each day's delay, and unless this is done, the delay should not be condoned, particularly, where valuable rights have accursed to the other side." 

 6. It is difficult to appreciate what weighed with the learned Judge in condoning the delay. At any rate, nothing is disclosed in the order. The learned Judge was manifestly unmindful of the relevant principles that should govern an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. When the delay was significant, it was also incumbent on him to notify the petitioner in whose favour a valuable right has accrued by lapse of time.
